    </defs>
    
    <!-- 白色背景 -->
    <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>

    <!-- 顶部渐变装饰条 -->
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="6" fill="url(#headerGrad)"/>

    <!-- 背景装饰 -->
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="720" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.02"/>
    <rect x="880" y="0" width="400" height="720" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.02"/>
    
    <!-- 几何装饰 -->
    <rect x="80" y="100" width="180" height="180" fill="none" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.08"/>
    <rect x="120" y="140" width="100" height="100" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
    
    <rect x="1020" y="420" width="180" height="180" fill="none" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.08"/>
    <rect x="1060" y="460" width="100" height="100" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.03"/>

    <!-- 主感谢语 -->
    <text x="640" y="230" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#005587" letter-spacing="4">
        THANK YOU
    </text>
    
    <text x="640" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="52" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">
        {{THANK_YOU}}
    </text>

    <!-- 装饰分隔线 -->
    <line x1="480" y1="340" x2="600" y2="340" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="3"/>
    <circle cx="640" cy="340" r="8" fill="#F5A623"/>
    <line x1="680" y1="340" x2="800" y2="340" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="3"/>

    <!-- 副标语 -->
    <text x="640" y="390" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#5D6D7E">
        {{TAGLINE}}
    </text>

    <!-- 联系信息卡片 -->

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Opening slide establishing the scope and data sources for the presentation. The deck covers 275 years of CO₂ emissions data from the Industrial Revolution through 2024, drawing from the Global Carbon Budget 2025 and NASA climate data. This sets the authoritative, data-forward tone for policy analysts and climate negotiators.

Key points: ① Comprehensive scope ② Credible sources ③ Professional context
Duration: 1 minute

---
# 02_atmospheric_co2

[Transition] We begin with the atmosphere itself — the ultimate receptor of all these emissions.

The latest Mauna Loa measurement shows atmospheric CO₂ at 429 parts per million as of February 2026. This represents a more than 50% increase from the pre-industrial baseline of approximately 280 ppm. The current level is at least 1.5 times greater than the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago — a change that took thousands of years then but has occurred in roughly two centuries now.

The acceleration since 1958 is striking: from 315 ppm to 429 ppm. This is not a gradual increase — it is exponential growth driven primarily by burning coal, oil, and natural gas.

Key points: ① 429 ppm — highest in 3 million years ② 50% above pre-industrial ③ Acceleration is the key story
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 03_six_fold_growth

[Transition] Now let's trace where these emissions come from — starting with the总量.

Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ emissions were negligible. Growth remained relatively slow until the mid-20th century. In 1950, the world emitted roughly 6 billion tonnes of CO₂. By 1990, emissions had nearly quadrupled to over 20 billion tonnes. Today, global annual emissions from fossil fuels and industry exceed 35 billion tonnes.

The key inflection point is China's rapid post-2000 industrial surge, which accounts for much of the recent growth. While emissions growth has slowed in recent years, they have not yet peaked — a critical finding for policy planners.

Key points: ① 6→20→35+ Bt trajectory ② Not yet peaked ③ China drives recent acceleration
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 04_china_surges

[Transition] The previous slide hinted at it — let's now look at who's actually emitting.

China is the world's largest emitter by a significant margin, producing over 12 billion tonnes annually — more than one-quarter of the global total. The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined to roughly 5 billion tonnes. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes.

The contrast is stark: China's ascent from negligible share in 1950 to 27% today represents one of the fastest industrial transformations in history. Meanwhile, Europe and the US dominated until the mid-20th century — their share has collapsed from over 90% in 1900 to below one-third today.

Key points: ① China 12.5 Bt (27%) ② US declining from peak ③ Dramatic geographic shift
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 05_regional_shift

[Transition] This geographic shift is so dramatic it deserves its own visualization.

In 1900, Europe and the US accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions.

Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined. This has profound implications for international climate negotiations: the countries doing least to cause the problem are least responsible for its solutions, yet face the greatest vulnerability to its effects.

Key points: ① 1900: >90% from Europe+US ② 2024: Asia ~50%, US+Europe <33% ③ Equity implications
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 06_per_capita_gap

[Transition] Total emissions tell one story. Per capita emissions reveal another.

Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The US, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average. The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately 150-fold: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year.

Critically, countries with similar living standards can differ significantly — France and the UK have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of their energy mix. This is not about prosperity alone — it's about policy choices.

Key points: ① 150× disparity (US vs Chad) ② US 3× global average ③ Energy choices matter
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 07_2024_snapshot

[Transition] So what does the most recent data show? A mixed picture.

The 2024 annual percentage change map shows a divided world. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines of roughly −1% to −5%, shown in blue. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more, shown in orange and red.

Some countries in South America experienced very large percentage increases — though from a small base. The net global effect is that emissions are still rising. The transition is underway but incomplete. US and European declines are real but insufficient to offset growth elsewhere.

Key points: ① US/Europe declining ② Russia/SE Asia/Africa rising ③ Net global emissions still growing
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 08_energy_mix

[Transition] The previous slide showed that declines are possible. This one explains why outcomes differ so dramatically.

The comparison between France/UK and Germany/Netherlands is instructive. France generates roughly 70% of its electricity from nuclear power, with another 17% from renewables — only about 5% from fossil fuels. This yields per capita emissions of approximately 4 tonnes. The UK has achieved similar results through renewables and nuclear, with significant coal phase-out.

Germany, despite being one of the world's leading economies, emits roughly 8 tonnes per capita because roughly half its electricity still comes from coal and gas — and it completed its nuclear phase-out in 2023. The Netherlands sits at around 9 tonnes per capita due to heavy reliance on natural gas and limited renewables penetration.

This is the same prosperity, very different choices — and vastly different outcomes.

Key points: ① France/UK: ~4 t (nuclear + renewables) ② Germany/Netherlands: ~8-9 t (fossil-heavy) ③ Policy trumps prosperity
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me synthesize what we've covered.

Five key findings: First, global CO₂ emissions now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth rates. Second, China alone accounts for over 25% of global emissions — more than double the United States — while India is rising fast. Third, the geographic center of emissions has shifted dramatically: from over 90% in Europe and the US in 1900 to Asia producing roughly 50% today.

Fourth, per capita inequalities are extreme — a 150× gap separates the highest emitters from the lowest. Fifth, and perhaps most importantly for policy, energy mix and policy choices matter: countries with similar prosperity levels can have very different per capita emissions.

For climate negotiators, this means effective policy must address both total emissions AND per capita equity — recognizing that historical responsibility, current capacity, and energy choices all shape the path forward.

Key points: ① 35+ Bt, not yet peaked ② China >25%, shift to Asia ③ 150× per capita gap ④ Energy mix determines outcomes ⑤ Policy equity matters
Duration: 3 minutes

The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined to roughly 5 billion tonnes. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes.

The contrast is stark: China's ascent from negligible share in 1950 to 27% today represents one of the fastest industrial transformations in history. Meanwhile, Europe and the US dominated until the mid-20th century — their share has collapsed from over 90% in 1900 to below one-third today.

Key points: ① China 12.5 Bt (27%) ② US declining from peak ③ Dramatic geographic shift
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 05_regional_shift

[Transition] This geographic shift is so dramatic it deserves its own visualization.

In 1900, Europe and the US accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions.

Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined. This has profound implications for international climate negotiations: the countries doing least to cause the problem are least responsible for its solutions, yet face the greatest vulnerability to its effects.

Key points: ① 1900: >90% from Europe+US ② 2024: Asia ~50%, US+Europe <33% ③ Equity implications
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 06_per_capita_gap

[Transition] Total emissions tell one story. Per capita emissions reveal another.

Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The US, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average. The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately 150-fold: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year.

Critically, countries with similar living standards can differ significantly — France and the UK have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of their energy mix. This is not about prosperity alone — it's about policy choices.

Key points: ① 150× disparity (US vs Chad) ② US 3× global average ③ Energy choices matter
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 07_2024_snapshot

[Transition] So what does the most recent data show? A mixed picture.

The 2024 annual percentage change map shows a divided world. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines of roughly −1% to −5%, shown in blue. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more, shown in orange and red.

Some countries in South America experienced very large percentage increases — though from a small base. The net global effect is that emissions are still rising. The transition is underway but incomplete. US and European declines are real but insufficient to offset growth elsewhere.

Key points: ① US/Europe declining ② Russia/SE Asia/Africa rising ③ Net global emissions still growing
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 08_energy_mix

[Transition] The previous slide showed that declines are possible. This one explains why outcomes differ so dramatically.

The comparison between France/UK and Germany/Netherlands is instructive. France generates roughly 70% of its electricity from nuclear power, with another 17% from renewables — only about 5% from fossil fuels. This yields per capita emissions of approximately 4 tonnes. The UK has achieved similar results through renewables and nuclear, with significant coal phase-out.

Germany, despite being one of the world's leading economies, emits roughly 8 tonnes per capita because roughly half its electricity still comes from coal and gas — and it completed its nuclear phase-out in 2023. The Netherlands sits at around 9 tonnes per capita due to heavy reliance on natural gas and limited renewables penetration.

This is the same prosperity, very different choices — and vastly different outcomes.

Key points: ① France/UK: ~4 t (nuclear + renewables) ② Germany/Netherlands: ~8-9 t (fossil-heavy) ③ Policy trumps prosperity
Duration: 2 minutes

---
# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me synthesize what we've covered.

Five key findings: First, global CO₂ emissions now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth rates. Second, China alone accounts for over 25% of global emissions — more than double the United States — while India is rising fast. Third, the geographic center of emissions has shifted dramatically: from over 90% in Europe and the US in 1900 to Asia producing roughly 50% today.

Fourth, per capita inequalities are extreme — a 150× gap separates the highest emitters from the lowest. Fifth, and perhaps most importantly for policy, energy mix and policy choices matter: countries with similar prosperity levels can have very different per capita emissions.

For climate negotiators, this means effective policy must address both total emissions AND per capita equity — recognizing that historical responsibility, current capacity, and energy choices all shape the path forward.

Key points: ① 35+ Bt, not yet peaked ② China >25%, shift to Asia ③ 150× per capita gap ④ Energy mix determines outcomes ⑤ Policy equity matters
Duration: 3 minutes

The 9-slide presentation has been created and saved to `/app/output/final_deck.pptx` (78.9 KB).

**Deck Summary:**
- **Slide 1:** Title slide with scope 1750–2024, data source attribution
- **Slide 2:** Atmospheric CO₂ milestone — 429 ppm (50% above pre-industrial)
- **Slide 3:** Global emissions trajectory — 6 Bt (1950) → 20 Bt (1990) → 35+ Bt (2024)
- **Slide 4:** National comparisons — China 12.5 Bt vs US 5 Bt
- **Slide 5:** Regional share shift — 1900 (>90% Europe+US) vs 2024 (Asia ~50%)
- **Slide 6:** Per capita 150× gap — horizontal bar chart (US 15t, Chad 0.1t)
- **Slide 7:** 2024 snapshot — US/Europe declining, Russia/SE Asia rising
- **Slide 8:** Energy mix comparison — France/UK (~4t) vs Germany/Netherlands (~8-9t)
- **Slide 9:** Key takeaways — 5 synthesized findings

All statistics and claims are grounded in source_brief.md (Global Carbon Budget 2025, NASA data).
